concept: Given a sorted array of integers and a target value, return the index of the target. If the target is not found, return -1.

solutions.label: Linear Search
solutions.summary: Scan every element from left to right until the target is found or the array ends.

solutions.label: Binary Search
solutions.summary: Use two pointers to repeatedly halve the search range by comparing the middle element with the target.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Input: nums = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11], target = 7"] --> B{"Find index of 7"}
    B --> C["Output: 3"]
    style A fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style C fill:#f87171,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Let's work on a search problem. You're given an array of integers that is already sorted in ascending order, and a target value. Your task is to find the index of the target in the array. If it doesn't exist, return negative one.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. Just to confirm, the array is always sorted and contains integers. Can the array be empty, or have just one element?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the array can be empty, in which case you return negative one. It can also have a single element. All values are unique, and the array is sorted in non-decreasing order.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So for example, given the array one, three, five, seven, nine, eleven and a target of seven, I should return index three. And if the target were four, I'd return negative one. Let me think about approaches.

sections.title: Linear Search
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    A["i=0: 1"] --> B["i=1: 3"] --> C["i=2: 5"] --> D["i=3: 7 ✓"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style D fill:#22c55e,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is a linear search. I loop through the array from left to right and check each element. If it matches the target, I return the current index.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Using our example, I check index zero which is one, not seven. Index one is three, not seven. Index two is five, not seven. Index three is seven, that's a match, so I return three.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity is O of n in the worst case, because I might need to check every element. The space complexity is O of one since I only use a loop variable. This works, but it doesn't take advantage of the sorted order at all.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Right. The array is sorted, so can you do better?

sections.title: Binary Search
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    S["Array: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11], target = 7"]
    S --> R1["Step 1: left=0, right=5, mid=2, value=5"]
    R1 --> D1{"5 < 7?"}
    D1 -->|Yes| R2["Step 2: left=3, right=5, mid=4, value=9"]
    R2 --> D2{"9 > 7?"}
    D2 -->|Yes| R3["Step 3: left=3, right=3, mid=3, value=7"]
    R3 --> D3{"7 == 7?"}
    D3 -->|Found!| RES["Return index 3"]
    style R1 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style R2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style R3 fill:#22c55e,color:#fff
    style RES fill:#22c55e,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Since the array is sorted, I can use binary search. I maintain two pointers, left and right, starting at the beginning and end of the array. I calculate the midpoint and compare the middle element to the target.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: If the middle value equals the target, I return mid. If the middle value is less than the target, the target must be in the right half, so I move left to mid plus one. If the middle value is greater, I move right to mid minus one.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me walk through the example. The array is one, three, five, seven, nine, eleven and the target is seven. Left is zero, right is five, so mid is two. The value at index two is five, which is less than seven, so I set left to three.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Now left is three, right is five, mid is four. The value at index four is nine, which is greater than seven, so I set right to three. Now left equals right equals three, mid is three, and the value is seven. That's the target, so I return three.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great walkthrough. What about the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each step cuts the search space in half, so the time complexity is O of log n. The space complexity is O of one because I only use a few variables. This is much better than linear search for large arrays.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison
        A["Linear Search\nO of n time\nO of 1 space"] ---|"Optimize"| B["Binary Search\nO of log n time\nO of 1 space"]
    end
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice work. Let's summarize. The linear search checks every element in O of n time. Binary search takes advantage of the sorted order to cut the search space in half each step, achieving O of log n time.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key takeaway is that whenever an array is sorted, binary search should be the first technique to consider. It's a fundamental pattern that appears in many variations during interviews.
